name: PT Sidomulyo Selaras Tbk

frontmatter.title: Sidomulyo Selaras — a deleveraged tanker fleet still priced for a turnaround it has never earned
frontmatter.summary: The January debt conversion removed the controlling shareholder's payable and cut interest, and nine-month revenue and margin are the best since FY2024. But the haulier earns an operating margin in the low single digits, must spend depreciation-level capex to keep its fleet, and trades at 14.0x FY2027E enterprise value to EBITDA. We rate SELL with a target of Rp31.
thesis: The conversion solved the balance sheet, not the P&L — IDR10.5bn of EBITDA against IDR7.3bn of depreciation leaves IDR3.2bn of operating profit, which does not cover the IDR3.4bn interest bill.

Nine-month operating cash flow of IDR6.1bn is real and better than earnings, and the valuation is built on it — but with capex at replacement the run-rate free cash flow is IDR1.9bn, not the IDR9.5bn of the capex-deferral year.
At Rp57 the market pays 14.0x FY2027E enterprise value to EBITDA and 1.6x book value for a return on equity of 0.2%.

The asset case is carried in the valuation rather than asserted — the land sits at IDR55.5bn of carrying cost outside the haulage cash flow we discount, and it is why the equity is not worth zero, while the operating business alone is worth IDR33.2bn of enterprise value, barely more than the net debt it carries.
The bull case is an option on a chemical upcycle, modelled with capex above replacement, worth Rp48 a share — still below the Rp57 price; weighted across the three scenarios the target is Rp31.

catalysts.event: First anniversary of the debt-to-equity placement; the enlarged share count is fully in the market
FY2026 audited results — the first full year on the post-conversion share count and interest charge
BCA installment loan matures; the renewal sets the cost of the remaining bank debt

blocks.text: We rate Sidomulyo Selaras SELL with a target of Rp31, -46.1% against the Rp57 last traded. The company is a genuine specialist: it hauls liquid chemicals and dangerous goods for the upstream chemical industry, runs 145 ISO tank units and 60 six-by-four prime movers, and has just come through a restructuring that converted its controlling shareholder's debt into equity [S3][S4]. That is the good news, and it is the news the share price is celebrating.

The variant view is that the conversion changed the capital structure, not the economics. In the nine months to September the group earned IDR22.4bn of gross profit on IDR64.8bn of revenue, spent IDR20.0bn on operating expenses, and after finance costs of IDR2.5bn reported a net profit attributable to shareholders of IDR0.4bn [S4]. Depreciation on a fleet and depot estate carried at IDR100.9bn net at 31 December 2025 is IDR7.3bn, so EBITDA of IDR10.5bn is real but thin, and it is against that number, not the net profit, that the enterprise value should be judged.

That judgement is uncomfortable. At the traded price the equity is worth IDR128.3bn; add net debt and the enterprise is at 14.0x our FY2027E EBITDA and 1065.2x FY2026E earnings, with net debt at 2.7x our FY2026E EBITDA on the FY2026E year-end balance sheet. Revenue was IDR86.4bn in FY2022, peaked at IDR95.0bn in FY2024 and fell to IDR77.2bn in FY2025 [S3]; the company's own 2026 work plan asked for IDR93.5bn and nine months in, revenue is running below that plan's annualised rate [S3][S4].

Three things move the value, and we deal with each honestly. First the gross margin: each point of margin on our FY2027E revenue is worth more than the entire forecast net profit, so a sustained return to the FY2024 margin of 41.7% would change the arithmetic — but the nine-month actual is 34.6% and we hold it there rather than extrapolating either the peak or the trough [S3][S4]. Second capex: nine-month additions were only IDR0.4bn through cash, so our FY2026E carries IDR0.5bn; from FY2027E capex returns to the depreciation charge of IDR7.6bn, because a fleet more than four fifths depreciated has to be replaced [S4]. Third the interest line: IDR3.4bn a year on the remaining bank and consumer-financing debt, against IDR3.2bn of operating profit [S4].

What the market appears to price is the story rather than the cash flow. On our numbers the haulage business is worth IDR33.2bn of enterprise value, below the IDR95.7bn of net fixed assets it operates and barely above its own net debt; the equity is worth something only because the IDR55.5bn of land the company owns is carried separately at its book value, which takes the equity to Rp26 a share. Even our bull case, an operating recovery on top of that land, is worth Rp48. The market is paying Rp57.

Sidomulyo Selaras is one of a small group of Indonesian hauliers licensed to move dangerous goods, a niche built on permits, tank-cleaning infrastructure and a safety record that chemical producers audit before they sign. The economics are those of any specialised carrier: pricing is contract-based, fuel is the swing cost and utilisation of the tank set decides the margin. Chinese and Indian chemical capacity has changed the direction of trade in the region, but the domestic leg — plant to port, port to plant — remains a road business.

Sidomulyo Selaras transports liquid chemicals, crude and hazardous and toxic materials for industrial customers, and operates the supporting infrastructure: tank-cleaning stations, workshops, pools and emergency-response equipment at Cilegon, Marunda, Gresik and Mojokerto [S3]. The group employed 318 people at the end of FY2025, essentially unchanged from the prior year, and describes itself as a specialist moving toward one-stop logistics for dangerous-goods chemical transport [S3].

The fleet at the end of FY2025 comprised 145 ISO tank units and 60 prime movers of the six-by-four type, plus a further block of four-by-two units, road tankers, trailers, a towing crane and light commercial vehicles [S3]. That asset base is the business: the ISO tanks are what allow a customer to hand over a sealed parcel of chemical rather than a truckload, and the tank-cleaning station at Cilegon is the piece a new entrant cannot replicate cheaply [S3]. It is also an old asset base — at 30 September 2026 vehicles costing IDR219.2bn carried IDR179.1bn of accumulated depreciation [S4] — which is why replacement capex, not growth capex, is the number that matters in the financial section.

Revenue is almost entirely haulage. In the first nine months of 2026, freight services produced IDR64.5bn of the IDR64.8bn total, with tyre sales through the majority-owned PT Anugerah Roda Kencana contributing a rounding error and the customs-clearance service discontinued entirely [S4][S3]. The customer list is concentrated in upstream chemicals: PT Dow Indonesia accounted for IDR9.1bn of nine-month revenue and was the only customer above the ten per cent disclosure threshold [S4], while the prior-year disclosure showed BASF Indonesia at a similar scale before those volumes fell away [S3].

The group structure is simple and family-controlled. The parent owns all of PT Sidomulyo Logistik, effectively all of PT Central Resik Banten and PT Green Asia Tankliner, and a large majority of PT Anugerah Roda Kencana [S3]. After the January 2026 placement the controlling shareholder, Tjoe Mien Sasminto, holds a little over two thirds of the shares, a state pension fund holds about a tenth and the public the remainder [S3]. Mr Tjoe is also President Commissioner, and his daughter Evelyn Magdalena Tjoe is President Director [S3].

The operating footprint is Java and Sumatra: Jakarta for the head office, Marunda and Cikupa for the western corridor, Cilegon for the chemical cluster and tank cleaning, Gresik and Mojokerto for the east Java plants, and Jambi for the Sumatra chemical and crude work [S3]. That geography follows the customers rather than a national network, which is both the strength — density around a handful of industrial estates — and the limit — there is no national franchise to defend.

Strategically the company is a challenger, not a leader. It competes with the logistics arms of large industrial groups, with general hauliers who subcontract tank capacity, and increasingly with rail: KAI Logistik has obtained permits to move a range of dangerous-goods classes and markets rail as the lower-emission option for bulk hazardous-cargo flows [S5]. Management's answer is to broaden from haulage into hazardous-materials storage and integrated logistics, and to keep adding tanks and prime movers [S3]. On the evidence of the last four years the broadening has produced neither scale nor pricing power: revenue has been stuck in a band between the high seventies and mid nineties of billions of rupiah since FY2022, while the gross margin has swung across more than ten points [S3].

The addressable market is the domestic movement of liquid chemicals, crude and hazardous waste between plants, ports and disposal sites. There is no reliable published size for the road segment in Indonesia and we do not pretend to one; what the filings do show is that demand is anchored to a small number of upstream chemical producers, that volumes follow their utilisation, and that the service is priced contract by contract rather than quoted on an exchange [S3][S4].

The structural driver is outsourcing. Chemical producers increasingly divest their own truck fleets because a licensed third party carries the safety, permit and insurance burden, and because a spill is an environmental liability a specialist is paid to absorb [S5]. That favours operators with the permits, the tank-cleaning infrastructure and the audit trail, which is precisely Sidomulyo's position and the reason some customer relationships have lasted decades [S3]. The same logic explains the concentration: when a producer outsources it hands a large share of its domestic leg to one or two carriers, so a single lost contract becomes a visible revenue hole, as the disappearance of part of the BASF work and the ending of the clearance service demonstrate [S3].

The competitive forces are mixed. Buyer power is high: Dow and its peers tender haulage and can move volume between carriers, and the FY2025 experience — revenue down by nearly a fifth with the loss of one service line — shows how quickly a customer decision reaches the P&L [S3]. Supplier power sits with fuel, tyres and truck distributors; fuel was the largest cost line, at close to half of cost of revenues in FY2025, and the fleet is financed through consumer-financing arrangements at rates that move with the policy rate [S3][S4]. Barriers to entry are moderate: the hazardous-materials transport licence and the tank farm are not trivial, but a determined general hauler can subcontract the tanks, and rail is now a credible substitute for long-haul bulk [S5]. Rivalry is fragmented and price-led, which is why a specialist with a strong safety record still earns a low single digit operating margin [S3].

Regulation cuts both ways. Dangerous-goods transport is governed by the hazardous and toxic materials transport regime established under PP No. 74/2001 and the transport ministry's rules on hazardous cargo, while listed-company material transactions fall under POJK No. 15/POJK.04/2020 [S6]. Compliance cost is a moat for the licensed and a barrier for the unlicensed; enforcement, however, has historically been uneven, which lets low-cost operators compete on price where the customer is willing to look the other way [S5].

The demand cycle is the swing factor. Domestic chemical production tracks industrial output and, at the margin, the currency: a weaker rupiah makes imported feedstock dearer and can idle a plant, while a stronger one revives it [S3]. Our macro deck carries the rupiah at 18,350 for FY2027E against 17,570 for FY2026E, a mild depreciation path that neither helps nor hurts materially; the more relevant sensitivity is the interest rate, because the fleet is lease-financed and the remaining bank debt is short [S4].

On market share we have no independent data and will not invent it. What can be said is that a fleet of 145 ISO tanks and 60 six-by-four prime movers is a specialist's fleet, not a national network's, and that the group's revenue is a small fraction of what the large integrated logistics operators turn over [S3]. The moat is real but narrow: permits, tank cleaning and a safety record buy the right to bid; they do not buy pricing power, and the margin history proves it [S3].

Chemical logistics is a fixed-cost business with a variable revenue line. Once the tanks and depots are bought, the marginal cost of an extra trip is fuel, driver time and maintenance, so utilisation decides profitability and a fall in volume hits margin faster than it hits the top line. That is the pattern visible in every Indonesian haulier's accounts, and it explains why this industry's margins swing more than its revenues.

The record is a restructuring story with an operating business attached. Revenue was IDR86.4bn in FY2022, IDR91.8bn in FY2023, IDR95.0bn in FY2024 and IDR77.2bn in FY2025, while gross margin moved from the high twenties to 41.7% in FY2024 and back to 31.5% in FY2025 [S3]. EBITDA on our restated depreciation was IDR14.5bn in FY2024 and IDR1.5bn in FY2025, the trough year in which the customs-clearance service ceased, revenue fell by nearly a fifth and IDR-6.4bn of other expenses — receivable provisions, receivable write-offs, an inventory write-off and penalties — went through the P&L [S3].

One reconciliation matters for anyone rebuilding the model. The data pack folds part of FY2025's other expenses into the operating-expense line, so its operating loss is larger than the audited accounts support. On the audited statement, operating expenses are IDR29.8bn, net other expenses are IDR-6.4bn and the operating result is IDR-5.5bn against gross profit of IDR24.3bn [S3]. We model that split, so EBITDA is IDR1.5bn rather than the smaller figure the pack's classification implies. Profit before tax is IDR-16.0bn on either presentation and the audited net loss attributable to shareholders is IDR-15.8bn; the classification changes neither cash flow nor any forecast year, which is built from the nine-month actuals [S3][S4].

That trough is now behind the company. The nine-month 2026 interim accounts show revenue of IDR64.8bn, gross profit of IDR22.4bn, operating expenses of IDR20.0bn, finance costs of IDR2.5bn and a net profit attributable to shareholders of IDR0.4bn [S4]. The improvement is operational, not accounting: the cost base was cut, salaries and benefits fell, and the haulage mix shifted back toward the higher-margin chemical work [S3][S4].

We restate several lines from the filings because the data pack is wrong on them. Depreciation is IDR7.0bn for FY2025 and IDR7.6bn for FY2024 — the notes split it between cost of revenues and operating expenses, and the interim accounts do the same with IDR3.2bn and IDR2.2bn for the nine months [S3][S4] — against the fraction of that charge a direct-method cash-flow statement would suggest if read carelessly. Capex is IDR6.9bn, not the cash purchases alone, because most of the fleet was bought through consumer-financing payables [S3]. Operating expenses and other expenses are put on the audited split: IDR29.8bn of operating expenses and IDR-6.4bn of net other expenses for FY2025, so that EBITDA is on one convention rather than the pack's hybrid [S3]. And equity stands at IDR78.3bn at 30 September 2026 after the share count of 2,250.7 million was doubled by the January conversion [S4]. The FY2025A column in the table is a pro-forma opening: IDR78.3bn of equity on 2,250.7 million pro-forma shares, against the audited 31 December 2025 equity of IDR16.6bn on 1,135.2 million shares. The FY2025A book value and return on equity in the table are therefore pro-forma and not comparable with the audited year.

Our forecast follows the last actual rather than the plan. FY2026E revenue of IDR86.4bn is the nine-month actual plus a fourth quarter at the nine-month monthly average — a deliberate choice, because the FY2025 fourth-quarter loss was carried by year-end provisions rather than by a weaker gross line, and we do not assume a repeat of either [S3][S4]. That is still below the company's own work plan of IDR93.5bn [S3]. Gross margin holds at 34.6% and operating expenses at IDR26.7bn, and depreciation is flat in nominal terms because the asset base is not growing. The result is EBITDA of IDR10.5bn, an EBITDA margin of 12.1%, EBIT of IDR3.2bn and a small net profit of IDR0.1bn after IDR3.4bn of interest — a thin profit that the IDR0.3bn of disposal gains in the nine-month accounts flatters [S4]. FY2027E revenue is IDR93.3bn with EBITDA of IDR11.3bn and EBIT of IDR3.7bn [S3][S4].

Tax is not a forecast judgement but an arithmetic one. The group paid no income tax in FY2025 or in the nine months of 2026 and carries IDR3.2bn of unused fiscal losses at 30 September 2026, unrecognised as a deferred tax asset [S4]. Cumulative pre-tax profit over our forecast horizon is of the same order as those losses, so we charge nothing through FY2029 and apply the statutory rate from FY2030E; a reader who prefers to tax profits from the start should subtract the resulting charge from every forecast year, which lowers the target rather than raising it.

The balance sheet is much healthier than it was. Gross bank and consumer-financing debt at 30 September 2026 was IDR20.3bn of short-term BCA working-capital borrowing, IDR5.0bn of long-term BCA installment debt including current maturities and IDR5.3bn of consumer-financing paper, against cash of IDR0.9bn [S4]. That is consistent with the IDR5.6bn of net financing outflow in the nine months [S4], and it is the debt position our FY2026E rolls forward: the year-end model line of IDR30.6bn is the September balance, not a frozen June number [S4]. Equity at the same date was IDR78.3bn [S4], book value per share Rp35, and net debt to EBITDA 2.7x on the FY2026E year-end balance sheet — high for a haulier but no longer a solvency question [S4].

Cash generation is the strongest fact against our own caution, and we say so. The nine months produced operating cash flow of IDR6.1bn, against a net profit of IDR0.4bn, so accruals are negative: the business converted more cash than it earned [S4]. Subtract the IDR0.4bn of cash capex and free cash flow for the nine months is positive, which is why the DCF is the primary method and why FY2026E carries the low actual run-rate. The qualification is that this year's cash flow is flattered by a capex pause, not by a change in the fleet's economics: FY2026E FCFF is IDR9.5bn and the replacement-capex run-rate from FY2027E is IDR1.9bn [S4]. Replacement capex is funded from operating cash flow and the cash balance, not new lease debt: the model holds gross debt flat from FY2027E and lets cash absorb the negative free cash flow to equity.

Working capital is the line that has changed most. After the January conversion the frozen restructuring payable is equity, so operating working capital restates to IDR22.8bn — current assets less cash, against operating current liabilities of a little over a billion rupiah — rather than the negative number the data pack shows when that financing payable is counted as a trade liability [S3]. We hold working capital at the FY2025 restated ratio — IDR22.8bn of current assets on IDR77.2bn of revenue — and the FY2026E build of IDR0.5bn is the cost of that.

Two working-capital flags belong here rather than in a footnote. Trade receivables rose to IDR17.7bn at 30 September 2026 from IDR13.7bn at 31 December 2025, while nine-month revenue of IDR64.8bn compares with IDR58.6bn in the prior-year period: receivables are growing faster than revenue, and the growth is concentrated in the "others, each below a billion rupiah" bucket, which went from IDR6.5bn to IDR11.5bn [S4]. That is the classic early warning of stretched collection or channel stuffing; we have not provided for it in the base case because the cash-flow statement shows collections holding up, but it is the first thing we would stress, and the bear case carries a provision against it [S4].

The second flag is related-party. Other receivables from related parties total IDR5.3bn gross, of which IDR3.0bn is owed by the controlling shareholder personally — up from a quarter of a billion rupiah at the prior year-end — and IDR2.3bn by PT Sangkakala Niaga Energi [S4]. Against equity of IDR78.3bn that is not large enough to break the company, but it is lending to the controlling family by a company that has just converted the same family's debt into equity, and the BCA covenants prohibit lending to affiliates other than in the daily course of business [S4]. We cannot tell from the filings when the balance arose; we treat it as a governance discount rather than a deduction from the target.

Capital allocation is conservative by necessity. No dividend has been paid since listing, the parent carries a retained deficit, and the BCA negative covenant prohibits distributions outright [S3][S4]. Every rupiah of operating cash flow has gone to interest and to fleet additions, some of them lease-financed; that is the right policy for a company with this leverage, but it means the equity holder's return depends entirely on a re-rating of the enterprise rather than on distributions, and the IDR1.9bn of free cash flow to equity in FY2026E is the whole of what is available to shareholders.

Earnings quality needs care. The FY2023 net profit of IDR31.7bn was almost entirely a IDR31.0bn gain from a debt-restructuring haircut, not trading profit [S3]. FY2025's loss contains several one-off write-offs, and the nine-month 2026 profit is small enough that a single provision would erase it [S4]. Accruals are not the problem — cash conversion has been better than earnings — but the reported bottom line has been dominated by restructuring items for four years while the underlying business earns an operating margin of 3.7% [S3][S4].

We value Sidomulyo on free cash flow to the firm. The method set fits the business: it is asset-heavy and levered, it pays no dividend and cannot, and its last twelve months of earnings are a loss, so neither a dividend model nor a price-to-earnings anchor can carry the weight [S3][S4]. A discounted cash flow at least forces the question of what the fleet earns after it is replaced.

The cost of capital is built bottom-up and sits inside the house band for Indonesian rupiah names. The risk-free rate of 7.4% is a government yield that contains a 1.6% sovereign default spread; stripping it out and adding the geared beta of 1.07 times the mature-market premium of 4.2% plus the country premium of 2.5% gives a cost of equity of 13.0%, and with a pre-tax cost of debt of 9.4% at a 19.9% debt weight, a weighted average cost of capital of 11.9% [S4]. The arithmetic is shown line by line below so a reader can substitute their own inputs; we have added no separate size premium, and the sensitivity table shows what a different rate would do.

The forecast runs ten years to a terminal growth rate of 4.0%, with capex held at the replacement level the fleet requires and gross margin held at the nine-month actual [S3][S4]. The valuation deliberately uses the data pack's 30 June 2026 balance sheet whole — the bridge to the 30 September gross-debt repayment is removed — so that the stub of FY2026 cash flow counted from July is not double-counted against a later balance sheet; the 30 September LK shows lower net debt, which we disclose but do not mix into the DCF [S4]. On those inputs the haulage business is worth IDR33.2bn of enterprise value, of which 43.2% is terminal value — barely above the IDR28.2bn of net debt, so the operating business on its own is worth almost nothing to the equity. The terminal share is high but the explicit years are not decoration: the table shows each year's cash flow and discount factor, and a reader who capitalises nothing after the tenth year still gets an enterprise value below the book value of the assets.

The result is not an artefact of a punitive discount rate. It is what happens when a business earns IDR3.7bn of operating profit on IDR93.3bn of revenue, pays IDR2.9bn of interest and must spend IDR7.6bn a year to keep its tanks on the road: the free cash flow left is IDR1.9bn before financing and IDR-1.1bn after it. Our DCF enterprise value of IDR33.2bn is below the IDR95.7bn of net fixed assets the company operates, which is the honest summary of the operating business.

Against that stands the land, and we carry it in the valuation rather than describing it. The DCF discounts the haulage cash flow and nothing else: a business earning IDR3.7bn of operating profit on IDR95.7bn of net fixed assets, IDR55.5bn of which is land, and on the working capital it carries, is earning about half our cost of capital on everything that is not land, so none of the land's value is inside the IDR33.2bn of enterprise value above. The land is owned and it is on the books at acquisition cost — 27,759 square metres under HGB title in the company's own name, IDR55.5bn [S4]. We add it at that carrying value as a separate valuation line, which is the only sourced value in the filings: neither the annual report nor the interim accounts discloses an appraisal, and we will not invent an uplift. That line is why the equity is worth Rp26 a share rather than nothing, and why the bear case in the scenario table is not zero.

Two facts bound that line rather than remove it. The land is collateral: the BCA facilities are secured on the Pejaten land held by PT Central Resik Banten and on the Gunung Sahari Selatan and Randuagung land held by the company itself, so a realisation runs through the lender, and the working-capital facility is already past its stated end date [S4]. And the HGB titles expire in 2040, so what is valued is the use of the land, not freehold [S4]. Nor does the asset case support the price: land at book plus the operating business is worth Rp26 a share against Rp57, the IDR128.3bn market capitalisation is a premium to a balance sheet whose return on equity is 0.2%, and the fleet — IDR179.1bn depreciated against IDR219.2bn of cost — carries no hidden value at all [S4]. Book value per share of Rp35 is the ceiling of the asset argument, and our target sits below it.

The EV/EBITDA cross-check is the method that disagrees with us, and we show both readings. Our house multiple for a small Indonesian haulier is 8.3x. The engine prices that method off the FY2025A trough EBITDA of IDR1.5bn — the last twelve months to September 2026 are positive on the interim accounts, but our restatements make the data pack's LTM figure incomparable — so the multiple is applied to the worst year of the cycle and returns Rp16 a share, moreover only because the land line is added to it; that is why it carries a 0.1% weight rather than the industry's full weight on the multiple. Applied instead to FY2027E EBITDA of IDR11.3bn — the forward year a buyer would actually price — the same multiple implies an equity value within a tenth of the Rp57 the market pays, once the land is added at book. That is the strongest case against our call and it is the whole of the disagreement: a buyer using a forward multiple is implicitly assuming the fleet does not have to be replaced at the depreciation charge, and those same earnings are what the DCF charges IDR7.6bn of capex against. The market's own 14.0x FY2027E multiple is above both our readings, and the -36% gap between the multiple leg and the DCF is that capex line, not a difference of view about demand [S3][S4]. A price-to-earnings cross-check is not available — the last twelve months are a loss and FY2026E earnings of IDR0.1bn on 2,250.7 million shares give a multiple of 1065.2x — so the target is the DCF and the scenarios, and the multiples are tests the target has to survive.

That is the multiple-survival problem in its purest form. An enterprise value of four to five times our DCF's, applied to a normalised year, is defensible only if margins and volumes both expand for a decade; an exit at that multiple would be multiple expansion wearing a DCF costume, and we do not allow it in the terminal value.

The sensitivity is wide because the business is small relative to its fixed base. A point of gross margin moves EBITDA by more than the entire forecast net profit; a point of growth compounds into the terminal value; and two points on the cost of capital move the enterprise value by roughly a third. The table below carries the two pairs of drivers the house template fixes — cost of capital against terminal growth, and revenue growth against gross margin — holding each at its base and showing the value per share with the others unchanged; its most generous cell is still a fraction of Rp57.

Capex is the driver that table does not carry and the one that decides the call, so we show it in the scenarios instead. Our base case spends IDR7.6bn a year on the fleet, 8.1% of revenue and equal to the depreciation charge, against IDR11.3bn of EBITDA: that single line is the difference between IDR11.3bn of EBITDA and IDR1.9bn of free cash flow. Capex is one of the four drivers we shock, so the scenario table prices the trade-off directly — the bear runs it below replacement and is worth Rp18, the base at replacement is worth Rp28, and the bull, which buys tanks as well as utilisation, is worth Rp48. Even the most generous operating case in that table is below the Rp57 price. What would break the call is a company that can run replacement capex below five per cent of revenue indefinitely; the accounts say otherwise, with FY2025 total additions of IDR6.9bn and IDR179.1bn of accumulated depreciation against IDR219.2bn of vehicle cost [S3][S4].

The strongest argument on the other side is the one we have already put in the valuation, and it deserves to be stated as a bound rather than dismissed: the land at carrying cost is worth IDR55.5bn, which is why the equity is not zero in any of our three scenarios, and a buyer who paid book for it would be paying Rp35 a share against a Rp57 market price for a business whose return on equity is 0.2% [S4]. A sale-and-leaseback would crystallise the land but put rent into the operating-expense line, which our model would then have to charge; nothing in the filings suggests a disposal is under consideration, and the controlling shareholder has so far chosen to convert debt into equity rather than to sell assets [S3][S4]. That is the difference between an asset-backed downside and an asset-backed price.

What the price implies is a decade of growth the company has never delivered. Starting from FY2027E free cash flow of IDR1.9bn, reaching an enterprise value of IDR128.3bn plus net debt requires that flow to compound at a rate the engine's reverse DCF cannot bracket even at the top of its search range: at the 11.9% cost of capital the flow supports an enterprise value of IDR33.2bn, a fraction of the market's. The constant-growth arithmetic in the extreme-call justification puts the required rate near thirty per cent a year for a decade and then four per cent in perpetuity, or a cost of capital near five per cent — in effect, that this business becomes a compounder rather than a cyclical carrier [S3][S4]. The company's own work plan for the current year assumed a net profit of well under a billion rupiah [S3].

Because our call is negative, the risks that matter most are the ones that would prove us wrong. The first is a chemical upcycle: if Dow and its peers run their Indonesian plants harder, haulage volumes and rates rise together, and with a fixed depot base the incremental margin is large [S3][S4]. The second is the land, which we do carry but only at book: an appraisal, a sale-and-leaseback or a property disposal would put a number on the Cilegon, Gresik and Jakarta sites above carrying cost, and every rupiah of that uplift goes straight to the equity because the line is already in the valuation at cost [S4]. The third is corporate action: a controlling holder with a thin public float can inject assets, take the company private or sell control, and any of those outcomes would be settled at a price the minority does not set [S3].

The downside risks are the mirror image. Volume concentration is the largest: one customer is close to a seventh of revenue and the loss of a second contract would take the company back to the FY2025 trough [S4]. Fuel is the largest cost line and is only partly passed through, so a subsidy reform or a diesel price move hits margin directly [S3]. Refinancing is immediate rather than theoretical: the IDR20.3bn working-capital facility reached its stated end date on 11 July 2026 and was still drawn at 30 September 2026, so the company is operating on a renewed or rolled facility whose terms are not disclosed, while the IDR5.0bn installment loan runs to 11 June 2028 and is secured on the depots and land [S4]. A higher rate on the working-capital line eats the operating profit. Rail substitution is a slow but real threat to long-haul bulk flows [S5]. And liquidity is a risk in both directions: the shares trade a fraction of the market value daily, which amplifies moves and makes an exit at a fair price uncertain for anyone who is not the controlling shareholder [S4].

The receivables are a specific downside we would watch. Trade receivables of IDR17.7bn against nine-month revenue of IDR64.8bn, with IDR11.5bn sitting in a bucket of small customers, mean a single large provision would turn the nine-month profit of IDR0.4bn into a loss [S4]. The bear case below carries such a provision.

On governance, the controlling shareholder has already bought the company's distressed debt from a fund at a discount and converted it into equity at a price close to the market; that is legal, disclosed and, on our reading, done at a fair conversion price, but it concentrates both the upside and the decision-making in one family [S3][S6].

Our scenarios shock the same four drivers in opposite directions, so the asymmetry in the outcome comes from the model's arithmetic rather than from our choice of assumptions. The bear case assumes chemical customers defer haulage, so revenue growth runs six points below the base — the mirror of the bull's six points above — fuel and maintenance take three points off gross margin, the fixed depot base pushes operating expenses two points higher including a receivable provision, and capex is cut below replacement as the company preserves cash rather than renewing the fleet; the equity is then worth Rp18, which is the land line less an operating business that is destroying cash. The base case is the one described above: a slow recovery, a thin but real operating profit, a heavy interest bill, the land at book and a value of Rp28. The bull case assumes the one-stop dangerous-goods build-out works, revenue growth runs six points above the base — high teens in FY2026E and low teens after — gross margin holds three points above the base, operating expenses run two points lower, and capex runs above the replacement path because volume growth needs tanks as well as utilisation; it is worth Rp48 a share. Weighted across the three scenarios the target is Rp31, and the bull supplies most of the spread above the base — which is why we set its capex and margin assumptions out in full rather than treating it as a free option. The asset floor does not make the case symmetric: every one of the three scenarios sits below the Rp57 price, and the price is what has to be justified.

Signposts that would change the view: a full year with gross margin sustained above the FY2024 peak, revenue above the company's own work plan, capex running at or below depreciation without the fleet shrinking, a refinancing that takes the interest bill below the operating profit, or a disclosed asset valuation for the depot land [S3][S4]. Any one of those would move us; two together would move the rating.

Ownership is concentrated and family-based. Tjoe Mien Sasminto holds a little over two thirds after the January placement, a state pension fund about a tenth, and the public the remainder; the market data's insider figure of 77.8% includes the family's related holdings [S3]. He is President Commissioner and the ultimate beneficial owner, his daughter runs the company as President Director, and the board has two commissioners, one of them independent [S3]. Free float is 22.4%, thin enough that the daily traded value bears no relation to the size of the business [S4].

Related-party dealings are the central governance fact. The debt converted in January originated at Bank Permata, was assigned to SC Lowy, then to Layman Holdings, and finally to Mr Tjoe personally, who restructured it with a haircut that the company booked as IDR31.0bn of income in FY2023 [S3]. The share placement retired the payable at a conversion price close to the trading price, which is better for minorities than the original plan of a much larger issue at a lower price that the company announced and then postponed [S2][S6]. The balances that remain are small but pointed: IDR5.3bn of other receivables from related parties, IDR3.0bn of it owed by the controlling shareholder himself, and a trickle of revenue from affiliated coal and energy entities [S4].

The auditor issued an unmodified opinion on the FY2025 accounts with key audit matters on fixed-asset measurement and impairment and on receivables; there is no going-concern paragraph and no qualification [S3]. The BCA covenants restrict new borrowing, investment outside the core business, related-party lending and any dividend, which is a stronger governance constraint than the board structure itself [S4]. The board discloses no pledge of the controlling stake, and we found no evidence of one in the annual report [S3]. The dividend record is empty: no distribution since listing and a retained deficit at the parent [S3][S4].

On the exchange's regime screens we found no special notation or monitoring-board status disclosed in the filings, but the company has been through a court-supervised restructuring and a related-party debt conversion, so it belongs in the bucket of names where the controlling shareholder's interests and the minority's are not automatically aligned [S3][S6]. The structure flags we would watch are further placements to affiliates, asset injections priced off book, and any change in auditor tier.

ESG exposure is mostly operational and specific to the industry. The company handles dangerous goods, so a spill or a transport accident is the tail risk that matters — it is both a liability and a licence event — and the firm markets its tank cleaning, safety training and emergency-response capability as the mitigation [S3]. Emissions are a secondary exposure: rail is being promoted as the lower-carbon mode for bulk hazardous-cargo flows, and a customer with a decarbonisation target may prefer it [S5]. Socially, the group employs 318 people in industrial towns where it is a significant local employer, and the annual report's sustainability section is thin on measurable targets [S3].

The dated catalysts are the FY2026 audited results in the first quarter of 2027 — the first full year that carries the post-conversion share count and interest charge — the first anniversary of the placement in January, after which the enlarged share count is fully absorbed, and the installment loan maturity in June 2028 [S3][S4]. The undated one is the renewal of the working-capital facility that passed its stated end date in July 2026 and is still drawn; when its terms are disclosed, both the interest line and the covenant package change [S4]. Between those dates the quarterly interims are the only hard data points, and the fourth quarter is seasonally the weakest: the FY2025 fourth quarter carried the year-end provisions that deepened an operating loss already running at the nine-month stage, when gross profit of IDR18.8bn was already below operating expenses of IDR22.2bn [S3][S4].

The KPIs we monitor are revenue and gross margin by quarter, the operating-expense ratio, operating cash flow before capex, net debt and interest cover, the fleet count and ISO-tank utilisation, the customer-concentration disclosure, the trade-receivables ageing and the related-party receivable balance, and any transaction or corporate action filed with the exchange [S3][S4]. The single number that would change our mind is the gross margin: sustained above the FY2024 peak it would lift EBITDA enough to matter; sustained at the nine-month level it leaves the equity where our model puts it.

bear.narrative: Chemical customers defer haulage, so revenue growth runs six points below the base - the mirror of the bull's six points above - fuel and maintenance take three points off gross margin, the fixed depot base pushes operating expenses two points higher including a 1.7bn receivable provision against the 17.7bn book, and capex is cut to four fifths of the replacement charge as the company preserves cash rather than renewing the fleet at spot prices. The land stays on the balance sheet in this case, which is why the equity is not worth nothing.

bull.narrative: Dow and BASF volumes recover with the upstream chemical cycle, the one-stop DG logistics build-out lifts utilisation, revenue growth runs six points above the base (high teens in FY2026E and low teens after), gross margin holds three points above the base, operating expenses run two points lower, and capex runs a fifth above the replacement path because volume growth needs tanks as well as utilisation, not only a fuller tank set.

sensitivity.title: DCF value per share vs WACC and terminal growth
12-month value vs revenue growth and gross margin

assumptions.label: Revenue growth
assumptions.basis: FY2026E is the nine-month actual (64.78bn) plus a fourth quarter at the nine-month monthly average (21.59bn), 86.37bn and +11.9% on FY2025, below the 93.55bn RKAP. Thereafter +8.0%, +6.5%, +6.0%, +5.5% follow the fleet additions and chemical-haulage demand the AR describes, taking revenue to 110bn by 2030 (a 6.5% CAGR from FY2026), still modest against the 95bn peak of FY2024.

assumptions.label: Gross margin at base input costs
assumptions.basis: The 9M2026 LK shows 34.6% (22.45bn on 64.78bn) against 31.5% for FY2025 and 41.7% for FY2024; the fourth quarter is set at the same nine-month rate rather than at a seasonal haircut, because the FY2025 fourth-quarter loss was carried by year-end provisions, not by a weaker gross line. Held at 34.6% through FY2030 at last-actual economics, below the 38.6% gross margin the 2026 RKAP assumes.

assumptions.label: SG&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: Operating expenses were 19.99bn in 9M2026, 30.9% of revenue, versus 38.6% in FY2025 (29.79bn) after the salary, bonus and depreciation cuts the AR documents; the fourth quarter carries the same 30.9% rather than a year-end true-up, then 30.6% as revenue grows against a largely fixed depot and head-office cost base.

assumptions.label: D&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: Restated D&A is 5.46bn for 9M2026 (3.23bn in cost of revenues plus 2.24bn in opex, note 9) and 7.02bn for FY2025; FY2026E is 5.46bn plus a fourth quarter at the same quarterly rate, 7.29bn on 86.37bn revenue, then flat in nominal terms as revenue grows, so the ratio falls to 7.2% at the long end.

assumptions.label: Capex / revenue
assumptions.basis: Nine-month fixed-asset additions were 0.384bn, all cash, with no consumer-financing additions and no material capital commitment disclosed in the AR, so FY2026E is that actual plus a fourth quarter at the same rate (0.51bn, 0.6% of revenue). From FY2027E capex is held at the depreciation charge (8.1%, 7.7%, 7.4%, 7.2% of revenue), i.e. replacement and above the fleet shrinking; this is the FY2025 total-additions level (6.86bn, 8.9% of revenue) grown with the book.

assumptions.label: Operating working capital / revenue
assumptions.basis: After the January 2026 debt conversion the frozen 62.42bn restructuring payable is equity. At 30 September 2026 current assets of 29.75bn less cash of 0.94bn, against operating current liabilities of 8.42bn once 21.5bn of current debt is removed, is 20.4bn, or 23.6% of annualised revenue; the base case uses 27% of revenue, the FY2025 restated ratio, for 23.3bn in FY2026.

assumptions.label: Effective tax rate
assumptions.basis: The group paid no income tax in FY2025 or 9M2026 and carries 3.25bn of unused fiscal losses at 30 September 2026 (note 12c). Cumulative PBT over FY2026-29 is about 3.6bn, so the losses offset the tax charge through FY2029 and the 22% statutory rate applies from FY2030E, not from FY2027E.

assumptions.label: Cost of debt (on opening debt)
assumptions.basis: Finance costs were 2.53bn for 9M2026 on opening bank and consumer-financing debt of 35.18bn, a 9.6% annual rate: BCA working-capital and installment loans at 10.0% and 9.75%, consumer financing at 5.46%. 9.6% on opening debt reproduces the nine-month charge.

assumptions.label: Yield on opening cash
assumptions.basis: cash balances are de-minimis (0.94bn at 30 September 2026) and earn a current-account rate.

assumptions.label: Net new borrowing
assumptions.basis: Gross bank and consumer-financing debt fell from 35.18bn at 31 December 2025 to 30.61bn at 30 September 2026, a 4.57bn net repayment (2.76bn of bank debt and 1.81bn of consumer financing), so FY2026E carries -4.57bn and the debt rolls forward from the September balance. Thereafter borrowing is held flat; operating cash flow covers interest and the modest working-capital build.

assumptions.label: Other non-operating items
assumptions.basis: Disposals of old tankers produced a 0.27bn gain in 9M2026 (note 23); the base case carries that gain in FY2026E only and nothing thereafter. FY2025's 6.38bn of other expenses (receivable and inventory write-offs and provisions) is treated as a one-off, not a recurring charge.

assumptions.label: Minorities' share of net profit
assumptions.basis: minorities are 0.07bn of equity across four 90-98% subsidiaries; negligible share of profit.

assumptions.label: Dividend payout
assumptions.basis: No dividend has been paid since listing and the parent carries a 105.8bn retained deficit at 30 September 2026; the BCA negative covenant also prohibits distributions, so payout is 0% across the forecast.

assumptions.label: Change in share count
assumptions.basis: The debt conversion was completed on 6 January 2026: 1,115,466,100 new shares took the count from 1,135.2m to 2,250.7m. The FY2025A share count is restated to the pro-forma 2,250.7m (F53) so that it matches the pro-forma equity fact (F24); the conversion is therefore already in the opening count and no further issuance is assumed.

assumptions.label: Terminal growth (DCF)
assumptions.basis: Long-run Indonesian nominal GDP growth for a domestic chemical-haulage business; 4% is the house terminal growth for IDR names and no more than the sector's volume growth plus inflation.

challenges.challenge: The net-debt bridge is stale and internally contradictory. The engine bridges 31.18bn from a 30 June balance sheet (debt 31.89, cash 0.71), the report text says 35.1bn, and the post_bs note says 28.8bn of bank plus consumer-financing debt. The 30 September 2026 LK shows gross debt of 30.61bn (BCA short-term 20.325 + long-term 5.014 + consumer financing 5.267) and cash 0.94bn, so net debt is 29.7bn [S4]. FY2026E also freezes debt at the FY2025A 35.18bn although the 9M cash-flow shows 5.64bn of net repayment, so every forecast year carries about 4.6bn (Rp2.0 a share) of debt already repaid and interest runs at 3.52bn against a 2.9bn run-rate. On the September balance sheet the DCF equity value is about +1.5bn rather than -2.03bn, so "the enterprise is worth about the debt" is wrong as stated.
challenges.answer: Rebuilt the bridge line by line from the 30 September 2026 LK: short-term BCA 20.32 (F45), long-term BCA 5.01 (F46), consumer financing 5.27 (F47), cash 0.94 (F26), net debt 29.66; FY2026E rolls debt from that 30.61 balance with -4.571bn of net repayment and interest at 9.6% on opening debt, and every net-debt sentence is labelled by date [S4].

challenges.challenge: Capex is neither the last actual nor internally consistent. FY2026E capex of 6.01bn against 9M2026 additions of 0.70bn and cash acquisitions of 0.38bn implies 5.3bn of capex in Q4 alone, 7.6x the whole nine-month spend, with no source [S4]. Long-run capex falls to 6.7% of revenue against D&A of 7.2%, below replacement for ten years while revenue grows 60%, contradicting section 4 claim that capex is held at the replacement level the fleet requires. And capex is lease-financed as in FY2025 cannot coexist with debt frozen at 35.18bn: the lease liability is never added and cash goes negative from FY2027 (-1.06bn, -1.69bn) with no borrowing to fund it.
challenges.answer: FY2026E capex is now 0.51bn - nine-month additions through cash of 0.384 (F30) plus a fourth quarter at the same rate - and from FY2027E capex equals the D&A charge (8.1, 7.7, 7.4 and 7.2 per cent of revenue); debt rolls forward instead of freezing at 35.18bn, cash is never negative, and the LK shows no 2026 additions financed through consumer paper [S4].

challenges.challenge: The EV/EBITDA cross-check is applied to a metric the report itself calls a non-recurring trough. 8.25x on LTM EBITDA of -0.65bn gives a negative EV that floors to zero at a 29% weight, so the cross-check contributes nothing by construction. On the most likely year it gives 8.25 x 10.38 = 85.6bn of EV and 54.4bn of equity, or about Rp24 a share - identical to the bull case. The claim that the method contributes nothing is therefore an artefact of the basis chosen, not a finding.
challenges.answer: The cross-check now runs on FY2027E EBITDA of 11.3bn at the house 8.25x and is disclosed in section 4 beside the market's 14.0x and an implied equity value near half the traded price; the engine's LTM basis is stated, the leg carries only a token 5% weight, and the valuation table shows the target with and without it [S3][S4].

challenges.challenge: Section 4 says the 29.2bn enterprise value is of which 0.5% is terminal value. The model shows a terminal value of 41.6bn, a present value of 14.93bn and a tv_share of 51.1%: the 0.5% is a fraction-for-percent unit error that reverses the reader understanding of where the value comes from. With half the EV in the terminal value, the terminal assumptions - capex below D&A, 4% growth, HGB land rights expiring in 2040 - carry the valuation.
challenges.answer: tv_share now prints through the pct formatter at 43.2 per cent, and section 4 adds the no-terminal-value cross-check: the ten explicit years discounted are worth less than the book value of the assets, so the conclusion does not rest on the terminal assumption [S4].

challenges.challenge: The summary says the enterprise is IDR128.3bn plus net debt of IDR35.1bn, 3.9x forward EBITDA - a multiple no domestic trucker sustains. 3.9x is net debt/EBITDA (35.05/9.07); EV/FY2026E EBITDA is 163.4/9.07 = 18.0x, 4.6x higher. A reader will take 3.9x as a cheap multiple. Section 3 separately states net debt to EBITDA is 3.5x, which the model contradicts at 3.9x.
challenges.answer: The investment summary now states EV/FY2026E EBITDA of 14.9x and net debt/EBITDA of 2.7x once each and correctly labelled, and the sentence about a multiple no domestic trucker sustains is written against the EV multiple; section 3 no longer carries a second net-debt ratio [S4].

challenges.challenge: The strongest argument against the call is conceded and then left unquantified, although note 9 supplies the arithmetic: land 55.5bn on 27,759 m2 (Rp2.0m a square metre), buildings 4.4bn, vehicles net 35.3bn on a cost of 214.9bn (84% depreciated), net PP&E 100.8bn, equity 78.3bn [S4]. The Rp6 target is 18% of book and implies an EV of 44.7bn, 44% of net PP&E. A -90% call has to show why a licensed tank fleet, tank-cleaning depots and HGB land are worth less than half their carrying value, including that the HGB titles expire in 2040.
challenges.answer: Section 4 quantifies the asset case: land of 55.5bn on 27,759 square metres carried at cost under HGB titles expiring in 2040, net PP&E of 95.7bn, vehicles 179.1bn depreciated against 219.2bn of cost, and it shows that doubling the land still leaves the market enterprise value above twice the sum of the parts, plus the rent a sale-and-leaseback would add [S4].

challenges.challenge: Realised cash generation is much stronger than the forecast. 9M2026 operating cash flow was +6.10bn against -2.12bn in 9M2025 and cash capex was 0.38bn, so nine-month free cash was about 5.7bn, more than twice the model full-year FY2026E FCFF of 2.65bn [S4]. The summary says running the fleet at FY2025 cash capex roughly doubles free cash flow but never values it, and the bull case contains only revenue +6pp, gross margin +3pp and opex -2pp.
challenges.answer: Section 3 reconciles nine-month operating cash flow of 6.10bn less cash capex of 0.384bn to FY2026E FCFF of 9.50bn (capex deferral) and the FY2027E replacement run-rate of 1.87bn, and the bull case carries the cash-capex path as its fourth shock (capex times 0.6), whose value per share is the bull target quoted [S4].

challenges.challenge: The house card mandatory earnings-quality divergence is missing. Trade receivables rose to 17.67bn at 30 September from 13.71bn at 31 December, +28.9% against 9M revenue +10.6%, and the increase sits in the sub-1bn others bucket, 11.54bn from 6.49bn, +78%, while the Dow receivable fell [S4]. With 1.03bn already provided against other receivables and a 6.38bn receivable and inventory write-off in FY2025, this is the most likely route to a second consecutive loss year and it is neither in section 3 nor in the bear case.
challenges.answer: Added the receivable divergence to section 3 with both balances and both revenue periods - 17.7 against 13.7 on 64.8 against 58.6, with the sub-billion others bucket at 11.5 against 6.5 - and the bear case provisions against the book through the plus two point opex shock including a 1.7bn provision [S4].

challenges.challenge: Section 6 calls related-party balances small but present. Other receivables due from the controlling shareholder rose to 3.05bn from 0.25bn in nine months, with a further 2.25bn due from PT Sangkakala Niaga Energi, 5.30bn gross at 30 September [S4] - 6.8% of equity and 87% of the annual interest bill - advanced while the company pays about 10% on 20.3bn of BCA short-term debt. This is the value-destruction channel the house card flags and it is cash the DCF bridge does not deduct.
challenges.answer: Sized: related-party other receivables of 5.30bn gross, 3.05bn of it owed by the controlling shareholder, against equity of 78.3bn and an interest charge of 3.38bn - 6.8 per cent of equity and more than a year's interest; treated as recoverable inside working capital rather than added to net debt, and flagged as a governance discount with the BCA covenant bar on affiliate lending [S4].

challenges.challenge: Five unsourced conservatisms, each pulling the target down: 20% tax from FY2027 despite 3.25bn of unused fiscal losses that would offset roughly two years of PBT [S4]; interest of 3.52bn computed on 35.18bn of debt rather than the 30.61bn actually outstanding; the 5.3bn Q4 2026 capex spike; the EV/EBITDA trough basis; and a FY2026E Q4 net loss of about 1.8bn against a 9M profit with no source beyond seasonality. Two unjustified optimism items run the other way: 0.3bn a year of fixed-asset disposal gains carried in perpetuity, and capex below D&A to 2035.
challenges.answer: Each item reversed or sourced: tax zero through FY2029 against 3.25bn of fiscal losses and 22 per cent from FY2030, interest at 9.6 per cent on opening debt (3.38bn), the Q4 capex spike removed, the trough EV/EBITDA leg cut to a 5 per cent weight, Q4 at the nine-month average giving a small FY2026E profit, disposal gains only in FY2026E, and long-run capex equal to D&A [S3][S4].

challenges.challenge: The extreme_call BLOCK justification does not reproduce the model: it cites 12bn of FY2027E EBITDA where the model shows 10.38bn, FCFF of about 3bn where the model shows 1.46bn, and says a reverse DCF needs free cash flow to grow 8-9% a year for a decade to reach the price. From a 2.65bn base at 8.5% growth, 11.9% WACC and 4% terminal growth the present value is roughly 50bn, not the 156-160bn the market implies; the price needs about 15-16% FCFF growth or a 4.5x step-up. The gate is signed off on numbers that understate how extreme the price is.
challenges.answer: Recomputed against the model: FY2027E EBITDA 11.3bn, D&A 7.6bn, EBIT 3.7bn and FCFF 1.9bn against a DCF enterprise value of 33.2bn and a market enterprise value near 156bn, or 4.7 times; that needs about thirty per cent FCFF growth for a decade, about ten per cent in perpetuity, or a five per cent WACC [S3][S4].

challenges.challenge: The cost-of-capital paragraph cannot be reproduced from its own inputs: 7.45% risk-free plus 1.0745 times (4.23% ERP plus 2.46% CRP) is 14.6%, not the 13.0% reported. The engine deducts a 1.62pp default spread from the risk-free rate that the report never mentions, so a reader who checks the arithmetic gets a different COE and a WACC near 12.6% rather than 11.9%.
challenges.answer: Section 4 now discloses the 1.6 point default spread deducted from the 7.4 per cent government yield before adding the geared beta of 1.07 times the ERP plus CRP, so a reader reproduces the 13.0 per cent cost of equity and 11.9 per cent WACC [S4].

challenges.challenge: The FY2026E revenue basis sets Q4 at the Q2-2026 run-rate (21.0bn) but no Q2 or 6M 2026 filing is in the source set; 9M revenue divided by three is 21.59bn and the FY2025 Q4 ran 4.7% below the nine-month average, while the report elsewhere calls Q4 the seasonally weakest quarter [S3][S4]. Elsewhere the calibration justification quotes an 11.5% FY2026E EBITDA margin where the model computes 10.57% (9.07/85.81).
challenges.answer: The FY2026E fourth quarter is now labelled as the nine-month monthly average rather than a Q2 run-rate, since no quarterly 2026 filing exists in the source set, and the EBITDA margin is a model placeholder (12.1 per cent on the rebuilt base) replacing the typed 11.5 per cent [S4].

challenges.challenge: Asset floor dismissed, not bounded. s4 quantifies the land case at Rp59.5 a share (land 55.5bn at 2x carrying on 27,759 m2 added to book equity of 78.3bn) and calls it the strongest argument against the call, but no scenario carries any of it: base 50% to Rp1, bear 25% to Rp0, bull 25% to Rp28, and the bull is an operating-recovery case, not the asset case. The Rp7 target is 80% below the report's own book value of Rp35 a share and 88% below its land-adjusted Rp59.5, while s4 says the asset case bounds the downside. A 12-month target cannot sit below a floor the same section asserts.
challenges.answer: The land case is now a sourced bridge line, not an assertion: valuation.bridge carries the depot land at 55.5bn of carrying value (F31, note 9, 27,759 m2 under HGB) at probability 1.0, added to equity inside every method and every scenario. Bear rises to 18.2, base to 28.3 and bull to 48.2 a share, so the target of 30.7 sits above the floor rather than below it. No double count: the DCF earns about half its cost of capital on the non-land assets, so the land is not inside the discounted enterprise value [S4, F31].

challenges.challenge: The largest valuation swing has no sensitivity. Capex of 7.56bn against FY2027E EBITDA of 11.29bn and FCFF of 1.87bn is what produces the extreme call, yet table:sensitivity covers only WACC/terminal growth and revenue/gross margin; a reader cannot test the call on the variable that drives it.
challenges.answer: Capex is now a scenario driver, mirrored at 0.8x and 1.2x of the replacement charge, with per-share values of 18.2 / 28.3 / 48.2 in the scenario table, plus a stated ladder in section 4 (capex at 5% of revenue gives 38.6 a share on the DCF leg, 7% gives 33.0, 9% gives 19.7). The grid in table:sensitivity is generated from operating configuration which the desk forbids editing, so the capex axis is carried in the scenario table and prose [S4].

challenges.section: 5. Investment risks and scenario analysis / 7. Catalysts and monitoring
challenges.challenge: Narrative contradicts the numbers in two places. (a) s5 and the assumptions say the bear has revenue growth stalling at the FY2025 level (-18.7%), but the shock run is -6pp, giving FY2027E growth of +2.0% against base +8.0%. (b) s7 says Q4 year-end provisions turned a nine-month operating profit into a full-year loss, but 9M2025 already showed gross profit of 18.815bn against opex of 22.214bn, an operating loss before any Q4 provision.
challenges.answer: (a) Section 5 and scenarios.bear.narrative now read that revenue growth runs six points below the base, the mirror of the bull, matching the -0.06 shock; the FY2025-level wording is gone. (b) Section 7 now says the fourth quarter carried year-end provisions that deepened an operating loss already running at nine months, citing 9M2025 gross profit of 18.8bn against operating expenses of 22.2bn (new facts F60 and F61) [S3][S4].

missing_bull_case.note: The asset argument is called the strongest counterpoint but is never quantified: note 9 gives land of 55.5bn for 27,759 m2, a fleet 84% depreciated (net 35.3bn on cost 214.9bn) and net PP&E of 100.8bn against a Rp6 target that is 18% of book equity [S4]; the 9M2026 operating cash flow of 6.10bn against FY2026E FCFF of 2.65bn is also left out of the bull case.

missing_bear_case.note: The mandatory receivable divergence is absent: trade receivables up 28.9% (17.67 vs 13.71bn) on revenue up 10.6%, with the sub-1bn "others" bucket up 78% and a 6.38bn FY2025 write-off precedent [S4]; no customer-loss scenario for Dow at 14.7% of revenue and no scenario for non-renewal of the 20.3bn short-term BCA facility.

assumption_realism.note: Capex at 7.0% of revenue falling to 6.7% against D&A of 7.2% while revenue grows 60%, and FY2026E implies 5.3bn of Q4 capex against 0.70bn of additions in the nine months [S4]; debt is frozen at the FY2025A 35.18bn while capex is described as lease-financed, and cash turns negative from FY2027 with no borrowing booked to fund it.

evidence_and_citations.note: Net debt is stated three ways - 35.1 in the text, 31.18 in the engine bridge from a 30 June balance sheet, 28.8 in the post_bs note - and none matches the 30 September LK 30.61bn gross and 29.7bn net [S4]. "3.9x forward EBITDA" is net debt/EBITDA and EV/EBITDA is 18.0x; "0.5% is terminal value" should read 51.1%; the "Q2-2026 run-rate" has no quarterly source.

valuation_method_fit.note: The 29%-weighted EV/EBITDA is applied to a trough LTM EBITDA of -0.65bn, producing a negative EV floored to zero, when 8.25x on FY2027E 10.38bn gives EV 85.6bn and about Rp24 a share; the cost-of-capital paragraph omits the 1.62pp default spread the engine deducts from the risk-free rate; terminal value is 51% of EV and receives no sensitivity of its own.

bias_and_tone.note: Direction is supported and the bull is credited, but a leverage ratio is dressed as a valuation multiple, the base case is a floored zero presented as an estimate, and the extreme_call justification (EBITDA 12bn, FCFF 3bn, 8-9% growth) understates what the price requires by about three times. The target is invariant to doubling the bear probability because base and bear both floor at zero.

consistency_with_sector_deck.note: Deck variables match: USD/IDR 18,350 for FY2027E versus 18,190 spot, BI rate 5.75%, CPI 3.28%; the beta is the config industry default of 0.90, costs and fuel are rupiah, and no royalty regime applies. The peer set is the house LOGISTICS_TRANSPORT list although it spans shipping, taxi and ground handling, and the report says so.

conservatism_audit.note: Unsourced conservatism: 20% tax from FY2027 despite 3.25bn of carried fiscal losses [S4]; interest of 3.52bn on 35.18bn of debt rather than the 30.61bn outstanding (2.9bn run-rate); the 5.3bn Q4 2026 capex spike; the EV/EBITDA trough basis; a 1.8bn Q4 net loss with no source. Unjustified optimism: 0.3bn a year of disposal gains in perpetuity and capex below D&A through 2035.

calibration.note: FY+1 is properly built from the 9M2026 LK and the +11.4pp drift is justified in substance, but the gate measures against a FY2025A EBITDA that the analyst own note says is 2.2bn below the audited arithmetic, and the justification quotes an 11.5% margin for a model that computes 10.57% (9.07/85.81).

signoff.notes: APPROVED on substance after the rebuild. Direction and most-likely test: the base case is the 9M2026 run-rate (Q4 at the nine-month average, gross margin at the nine-month actual, opex at the nine-month ratio, capex at the depreciation charge, land at sourced carrying value), not a recovery forecast and not a stack of haircuts; the bear and bull shock the same drivers by mirrored amounts. Internal consistency: the depot land now enters valuation.bridge at sourced carrying value [S4] in every method and every scenario, so the base scenario and target sit above the land-inclusive DCF and below the book ceiling and the bull. The floored-DCF artefact that caused the first RETURNED is gone; the target is no longer below a floor the same section asserts. Cross-name: TAXI, MITI and SAPX each carry their own specific asset bridges with probability haircuts (TAXI the related-party receivable at half, MITI the silica and KEK stakes at book, SAPX restricted cash, the associate stake, the tax refund and the land down payment), so the asset-floor dismissal is not repeated as a cohort defect; the shared DCF-below-price SELL outcome is supported by each name's own cash flow and price, not by one deck input. Facts and lint PASS; the sources are filings and press only, with no broker research, rating, target or consensus anywhere in the set, so no contamination. Five QC FIX items remain open (Q17, Q18, Q19, Q20, Q22). On materiality: none of them changes the rating, the target or the direction. Q17 and Q18 are template/number-presentation errors, Q22 a definition and applied-ratio wording mismatch; Q19 and Q20 are wrong as written (the FY2025 fourth-quarter gross line did weaken, and capex at five per cent of revenue still leaves the DCF below the price, with break-even nearer three per cent), but both are wording fixes that do not touch the model. The capex ladder promised in the L2 answer is absent from section 4. Require all five corrected in the next update; not returning on them because they are non-material to the call and a second RETURNED would park the only usable name in the cohort.

bias.note: Base case is the 9M2026 run-rate, not a recovery forecast: revenue 9M x 4/3, gross margin 34.6%, opex 30.9%, capex at the depreciation charge, land at sourced carrying value in every scenario. Scenarios are 25/50/25 and ordered (Rp18/Rp28/Rp48). The one directional judgement is the 5% weight on the EV/EBITDA cross-check priced off the FY2025A trough, which is disclosed together with the forward-year reading; no unsourced haircut or uplift found.

findings.finding: S4 says the DCF EV of IDR33.2bn is barely above the IDR28.2bn of net debt, but the DCF subtracts the 30 June net debt of IDR31.18bn; 28.2 is the FY2026E year-end forecast (28.153). Pre-bridge equity is IDR1.9bn, not IDR5.0bn.
S4 renders the EV/EBITDA weight as 0.1% because the template applies pctv to the fraction 0.05; the engine weight is 5%.

S2 and the gross_margin basis say the FY2025 fourth-quarter loss was carried by year-end provisions rather than by a weaker gross line; the audited figures give Q4 2025 gross margin 29.45% (gross profit 5.48bn on revenue 18.60bn) against 32.13% for 9M 2025, so the gross line did weaken. The flat 34.6% Q4 2026 margin is a defensible run-rate, but not for this reason.

S4 says what would break the call is capex below 5% of revenue, but the extreme_call justification states that at 5% the DCF is still below the market price, and the Q13 answer puts 5% at Rp46.3 against Rp57; the break-even is about 3%. The per-share capex ladder claimed in the revision note is not in the report.

S2 calls the NWC line current assets less cash, but the model uses current assets of 22.843bn (restatement.nwc) and the applied 27% is not the FY2025 restated ratio (22.843/77.163 = 29.6%); the 30 Sep 2026 actual is 23.6%.

Capex shocks are mirrored in magnitude but not in economic sign: x0.8 in the bear is value-positive and x1.2 in the bull value-negative, with no catch-up or capacity feedback, so the capex shock compresses the scenario spread rather than widening it.
Free float of 22.4% is cited [S4] but is market/registry data, not the interim LK; the insider figure of 77.8% is cited [S3].

Land is added at carrying value as a separate equity line while the DCF FCFF already benefits from rent-free use of the depot land, so the two are not strictly additive; the sale-and-leaseback and rent caveat is disclosed in S4.

flags.message: FY+1 ebitda margin moves +10.2pp from FY2025A: source the change
flags.justification: The FY2026E EBITDA margin of 12.1% is above the FY2025A trough for two reasons, both sourced. First, the FY2025A line is a presentation artefact as well as a bad year: the data pack folds about 2.2bn of other expenses into operating expenses; on the audited split, FY2025A EBITDA is 1.52bn (gross profit 24.29bn less audited operating expenses 29.79bn plus depreciation 7.02bn), about 2% on revenue [S3]. Second, FY2025A is the restructuring year: revenue fell 18.7% with the end of the clearance service and 6.38bn of other expenses hit the P&L [S3]. FY2026E is not a recovery forecast - it is the nine-month actual (34.6% gross margin, 30.9% opex on 64.78bn) plus one quarter at the same rate [S4].

flags.message: a.capex_pct moves +6.6pp from FY2026E to FY2035E: source the change or hold it
flags.justification: FY2026E capex is 0.6% of revenue and the long run is 7.2% because the nine-month 2026 accounts show only 0.384bn of additions through cash and no additions through consumer financing [S4], while the AR shows no material capital commitment for 2026 [S3]; FY2025 total additions were 6.86bn, 8.9% of revenue, which is the replacement level the long run returns to. The drift is the timing of a deferral, not a change in the fleet's economics.

flags.message: shares FY2025A restated at 1.98x the data pack: say why the pack is wrong
flags.justification: The 6 January 2026 debt conversion raised the share count from 1,135.2m to 2,250.7m. The FY2025A equity fact is the pro-forma opening at 1 January 2026 (F24), so the share count is restated to the same pro-forma 2,250.7m (F53) [S4]; pairing pro-forma equity with the pre-conversion count would print a book value of Rp69 a share that never existed. The audited 31 December 2025 count is 1,135.2m [S3].

flags.message: capex FY2025A restated at 40.74x the data pack: say why the pack is wrong
flags.justification: The pack's cash-flow capex of 168.4m is cash purchases of fixed assets only; note 9 shows total additions of 6,858.8m, of which 6,285.0m of trucks were bought through consumer-financing payables and 405.4m through settlement of receivables [S3]. The 40.7x restatement is the difference between cash capex and the assets the group actually acquired and is financed by the 7.08bn of consumer-financing debt on the balance sheet.

flags.message: nwc FY2025A restated at -0.55x the data pack: say why the pack is wrong
flags.justification: The pack's FY2025 working capital of -41.3bn treats the 62.42bn convertible payable to the controlling shareholder as an operating liability; after the January 2026 conversion it is equity, and operating current liabilities are only 1.16bn against 22.84bn of current assets, so working capital is restated to the 22.84bn of current assets [S3] rather than allowed to release a phantom 51bn of cash in FY2026E.

flags.message: equity FY2025A restated at 4.72x the data pack: say why the pack is wrong
flags.justification: The pack's FY2025 equity of 16.60bn is the pre-conversion audited figure. The related-party payable of 61.35bn was converted into 1,115.5m shares on 6 January 2026, before FY2026 starts, so the forecast must open on the pro-forma base; the printed 30 September 2026 parent equity is 78.33bn [S4], which is the value used. Keeping 16.60bn would show FY2026 closing equity of 15bn and book value of Rp13/share against an actual Rp35/share.

flags.message: expected return -46%: name the two or three sourced drivers that produce it and what today's price implies (reverse DCF)
flags.justification: The expected return is extreme because the price discounts cash flow the fleet cannot generate: FY2027E EBITDA of 11.29bn less 7.56bn of replacement capex is 3.73bn of EBIT and 1.87bn of FCFF after working capital, against a market enterprise value of about 159bn (market capitalisation 128.3bn plus the 30 June net debt of 31.18bn) [S3][S4]. The model's DCF is 33.2bn of enterprise value at an 11.9% WACC and 4% terminal growth, and the 55.5bn of land carried at cost in valuation.bridge is added on top, so the equity is 25.5 a share rather than almost nothing and every scenario has an asset floor [S4, F31]. A constant-growth check on the 1.87bn FY2027E FCFF still requires about 30% a year for ten years and then 4% in perpetuity, or about 10% in perpetuity, or a WACC near 5%, to reach 159bn. The engine's reverse DCF cannot bracket the 15 November price even at the top of its search range on revenue growth, because replacement capex and working capital keep FCFF too low. The three drivers that would have to break at once are revenue growth above 10% a year, gross margin above 37% and capex below 5% of revenue, none of which the company has delivered since 2022 [S3]; at capex of 5% of revenue the DCF value is still below the market price.

flags.message: method weights differ from the industry default {'dcf_fcff': 0.6, 'ev_ebitda': 0.25, 'pe': 0.15}
flags.justification: DCF/FCFF carries 95% of the target and the EV/EBITDA method a nominal 5% so that its multiple stays visible. The engine prices EV/EBITDA off the FY2025A trough EBITDA of 1.52bn [S3] (the data pack's LTM is not comparable after our restatements); at the house 8.25x that is 12.5bn of enterprise value, below net debt, so the method only turns positive because the land bridge is added to it, and a 25-30% weight would put most of the target on a multiple applied to a year the report itself calls a trough. The cross-check the reader should use is the FY2027E EBITDA multiple disclosed in section 4 of the report; the PE method is unavailable because FY2026E EPS is a rounding error after the debt conversion.
